newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's external deficit soars in August.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's external deficit soars in August.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday announced a record monthly current account deficit of $3.5 billion for August, swollen by falling prices for key exports, including semiconductors, steel and petrochemicals.
Bank of Korea figures showed the deficit for the first eight months of the year soared to $15.24 billion, more than double the bank's original projection of a $7 billion shortfall for the whole year.
A central bank official said there was "no short-term remedy" for the deficit that private economists predicted could hit $20 billion this year.
August's deficit was an increase on the July shortfall of $2.3 billion. It was also bloated by a rising invisible trade deficit, partly the result of a boom in Koreans travelling overseas on holiday.
"I'm getting worried," said Kim Gi-hyung, an economist at Daewoo Economic Research Institute. The trade deficit was combining with an economic downturn and the result could be recession, he said.
Lee Young-man, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute, said: "Under a worse-case scenario the deficit could reach $20 billion for the whole of this year."
Private economic think-tanks put the whole-year deficit at $18 to $20 billion. Last year's shortfall was $8.5 billion.

"We are working on the revision for the 1996 deficit forecast. Our figure will not show big differences with that of private economic institutes," said a Bank of Korea economist, who declined to be named.
"The huge deficit is expected to continue next year as there is no short-term remedy to improve it quickly."
However, he added that at $18 to $20 billion, the deficit would be still manageable at around three percent of gross national product.
Private economists predict next year's deficit at between $15.2 billion and $18 billion.

Bank of Korea figures showed that international prices of semiconductors, which account for nearly 20 percent of exports, fell by 72.3 percent in August year-on-year. Prices for steel products and petrochemical goods dipped by 13.8 percent and 16.7 percent respectively.
"The price fall is out of our control. It cannot be solved overnight," said LG Economic Research Institute's Lee.

The government is pressing a campaign to bring down costs by reducing prices and wages. It plans a freeze on government hiring next year, a clampdown on pay for senior officials and a reduction in utility charges.
It is also trying to improve corporate competitiveness, partly by bringing down high interest rates.
Kim of Daewoo said South Korea's reliance on imported raw materials and capital equipment made it particularly vulnerable to cyclical declines in the price of exports.
Despite the seven percent fall of the local currency against the dollar this year, Korean products have been hit by a weakening yen. Korea and Japan compete against each other with similar products.
Economists said the impact of the won's depreciation would show up from early next year, but the falling yen had already offset much of the potential competitive gains.
"We have to do something to make our products more value-added as we cannot survive by selling on price," the central bank economist said.
